card.name: Clause breaks in old literary and dictionary text
card.fires_on: Commas, semicolons, colons and the word "and" that join clauses in archaic poetry, old prose, and dictionary definitions. It fires where a new clause or an elaboration is about to begin.

modes.label: Joiner in poetry or old prose
modes.description: The word "and" or a comma after a clause in verse or 19th-century prose.
modes.example: I hear it now,<< and>> o'er and o'er, Eternal

modes.label: Punctuation in dictionary entries
modes.description: A semicolon or comma that separates a short definition from a further gloss.
modes.example: A kind of whitlow<<;>> a painful imflammation of the peri

card.plain: It marks the joint between clauses in old poems and dictionary definitions, where the text goes on to add more.
evidence: I hear it now,<< and>> o'er and o'er, Eternal
To sing so wildly<<:>> let us go.

contexts: One set slow bell will seem to toll The passing of the sweetest soul That ever look'd with human eyes. I hear it now,<< and>> o'er and o'er, Eternal
